chapter: Young players, schools and studio work
title: Outgrowing your influences; knowing the heritage
summary: A jazz player must stop copying and develop his own voice, but Hinton insists musicians know their heritage.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: But see, I think also then when a black musician gets good and he gets his own style going, he becomes creative, he doesn't listen any more anyhow, because he's got his own thing going now, his own creativity and --

Well, I can understand that because music is very jealous. In order for one to create, one can't spend too much time listening to something else because it might detract, it might detract from what you're doing.

It's very dangerous. You know, in the beginning you have to -- just like a child has to learn to speak by copying his mother and father's speech patterns, but at a certain point, much to the parent's disappointment, the child starts speaking for himself. And I think a good jazz player has to do that. And I can speak from experience that sometimes you can hang on to your mother's apron strings too long.
Agreed. I wasn't speaking of that
in terms of maturity, but I was speaking in terms of we should all know our musical heritage.

We should all know from whence we came. And if we like jazz, we should be familiar with who played and how. And anyway we can find out how it came about, then experience this anyway we can. And there are some excellent writers, some very excellent books that one can find this out. And there are still some old dudes around that you can sit down within sound of their voices and listen to their stories in their own way about what happened. And it would give us a sense of inspiration to carry on and be inspired. The roots type thing.
